title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (October 2027) — the edition the Winter Fuels Outlook is derived from, on a Columbus-Day-shifted Wednesday inside October expiration week
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, re-fetched direct 2026-09-08 by this event's own initial research (HTTP 200, 54,906 bytes — byte-identical to the eia-steo-2026-11-10 session's fetch) and re-parsed cell-by-cell. Its October 2027 row reads, verbatim by cell, `['October 2027', '10/13/2027', 'Winter Fuels Outlook']`; the November 2027 row reads `['November 2027', '11/09/2027', '']`. Release window stated on the same page as 12:00-12:15 pm ET. THE DATE IS DOUBLY DERIVED. The page's stated rule is "the release of the STEO on the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month", with the verbatim footnote "If a Federal holiday falls on the Monday before the normal release date the release is delayed until Wednesday." 2027-10-07 is the first Thursday, so the plain rule yields Tuesday 2027-10-12; the Monday before is 2027-10-11, which is Columbus Day. INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED FROM A NON-EIA FEDERAL PRIMARY fetched direct by this session: federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/k8.htm (HTTP 200, 82,205 bytes, page's own 'Last Update: July 8, 2026') carries the row `['Columbus Day', 'October 12', 'October 11', 'October 9', 'October 8', 'October 14']` for 2026-2030, putting Columbus Day 2027 on October 11 — and October 11 is the second Monday of October 2027 by arithmetic. So the table cell and the rule-plus-footnote agree, and the one-week-later-than-usual look is fully explained by the holiday. Filed estimate on two counts, neither of them date doubt: this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA (the standing schema gap eia-steo-2026-09-09 named), and this lane never self-confirms an event it discovered in-sweep. Checked 2026-09-08
notes: CANONICALISED 2026-09-08 by this event's own never-assessed initial research (docs/research/events/eia-steo-2027-10-13.md), promoting the sole prior proposal eia-steo-2027-10-13.from-eia-steo-2026-11-10.json — and AMENDING its headline claim, which is this session's main finding. The proposal titled this "the Winter Fuels Outlook edition", carrying forward the November sibling's correct fix that the Winter Fuels Outlook is an OCTOBER product rather than a November one. That fix stands. What did not survive is the implicit second half of it — that the October STEO release date is therefore the date the winter product lands. IT IS NOT, ON EIA'S OWN PRIMARIES. The Winter Fuels Outlook is a SUPPLEMENT DERIVED FROM the October STEO, and its own publication date floats: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/report/perspectives/2025/10-winterfuels/article.php (fetched direct this session, HTTP 200, 139,441 bytes) is headed 'Winter Fuels Outlook 2025-26 / as published on October 15, 2025' and states in its own body 'The data values and analysis below were published on October 15, 2025, and were based on price and weather forecasts from the October 2025 edition of the [STEO]' — while EIA's live STEO Archives listing (eia.gov/outlooks/steo/outlook.php, fetched direct this session, HTTP 200, 173,992 bytes) shows the October 2025 STEO itself released 10/7/2025, and the archived 2025 schedule table (web.archive.org snapshot 20251201193150 of the same release_schedule.php URL, HTTP 200, 84,780 bytes) carries `['October 2025', '10/07/2025', 'Winter Fuels Outlook']`. So in 2025 the Notes cell said October 7 and the winter product shipped October 15 — an EIGHT-DAY gap. In 2024 the two coincided (the 2024-25 article's tables are labelled 'Release date: October 8, 2024', the October 2024 STEO date). n=2, split 1-1. Consequence for this calendar, stated plainly: the 'Winter Fuels Outlook' string in the Notes cell marks WHICH EDITION the supplement is built from, not a guarantee it publishes that day, and no date-keyed reading of this entry may assume the winter numbers exist at 12:15 pm ET on 2027-10-13. A SECOND, PURELY MECHANICAL FINDING about the source itself. Across all 24 rows of EIA's live 2026-2027 table, five deviate from the plain rule: four are +1 day for a Federal holiday on the preceding Monday (09/09/2026 Labor Day, 07/07/2027 Independence Day observed, 09/08/2027 Labor Day, and THIS row) and one is +7 (01/13/2026, an unstated New Year exception that repeats in the archived 2025 table at 01/14/2025). EIA annotates the holiday-shifted Wednesdays '(Wednesday)' in the release-date cell — 09/09/2026, 07/07/2027, 09/08/2027 all carry it, as does 11/12/2025 in the archived table. 10/13/2027 IS A WEDNESDAY AND CARRIES NO ANNOTATION: it is the only holiday-shifted row in either table that EIA failed to label. The date cell is what this entry trusts, because the rule-plus-footnote reproduces it exactly and the Fed's own K.8 confirms the holiday; the missing annotation is recorded as a source inconsistency, not as date doubt. 2027-10-13 also falls OUTSIDE the same page's stated 'normally appear between the 6th and the 12th of the month' window — one of only two dates in the live 24-month table that do, the other being 01/13/2026, and both are holiday artifacts. THE CORRIDOR IS ALREADY ON THIS CALENDAR AND IS THE SAME HOLIDAY: sifma-bond-holiday-close-2027-10-11 (the Columbus Day bond close that CAUSES this Wednesday), opex-2027-10-15 (medium, CONFIRMED — this STEO publishes into October expiration week, two days before the monthly expiration) and fomc-blackout-start-2027-10-16 three days after, with fomc-minutes-2027-10-06 a week before. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning and the corridor does not raise it: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape, this calendar's names are `symbols: []` away from it, and the two 5-day neighbours that do carry flow (expiration, blackout) own their own days. The eleven other 2027 STEO dates visible on the same table are again DELIBERATELY NOT proposed, on the reasoning eia-steo-2026-11-10 recorded and this session re-confirmed: a measured null does not earn eleven low-impact research jobs.
